20 Äd3 Vg5+
This move simplifies White's task somewhat. However, Black could not have
saved himself even by 20...Qc4 which contains the transparent trap 21 Xb3?
Vg5+ 22 •bl Qd2+. At the time Lasker had reckoned on defeating 20...Qc4 in
the following manner (and this has found its way into the commentaries): 21
Nel? (in order to be able to meet 21...Vg5+ with 22 Äe3) 21...Äd6 22 Q)xd6
Vxd6 23 Äb3+ 06 24 a4 Ac8 25 xe8 Vd7 26 Vb5 Vxb5 27 xxb5 #b7? 28
Ad7 29 Xxf8 Äxf8 30 Xb4 and White goes on to capture the knight, after which
he is a pawn up in the ending. Let us disregard any doubts about this ending, for
Black has a stronger continuation than 27...#b7, namely 27...Ag7 28 Äxh8
Axh8; then White must play 29 a5 (otherwise the knight remains alive on b6)
whereupon the main line runs 29...Axd4 30 axb6 c6 31 Xb3 Axf2 32 b7 (if
White allows ...Éb7, then the position is still more favourable for Black)
32...Ae6 33 Éd2 c5! 34 c4 35 Äa3 Ad4, and it is clearly White rather than
Black who has to struggle for a draw. It is interesting to see how the original char-
acteristic of the position (the inability of the knight on h4 to move) again emerges
as the decisive factor as soon as the attack on the castled position peters out. Not
even the best players are immune from such misfortunes!
This game, which was the decisive one in Lasker's victory at St. Petersburg,
cannot be left to go on sleeping in the archives of chess history with an inaccurate
commentary. Good games should not be allowed to go to their rest without good
annotations as their lullabies! Therefore, we must show how in fact White does
win after 20...Qc4 (D).
So that there will be no doubt about it, we shall supply two winning moves,
both of them instructive as far as carrying out an attack in this kind of position is
concerned.
